name: Marco Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Marco. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We don't work for tech firms, employers or government, and anything you say is confidential. What does a normal working week look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play trumpet. From Easter to October I'm in the house band at the theme park outside town, four shows a day in a pirate costume, which is as silly as it sounds. Two days a week I teach brass at three schools for the county music service, on a temporary contract. On Tuesday nights I play in the town brass band, which pays nothing but it's where I learned.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the kids who come in thinking trumpet is impossible and play their first scale by Christmas. The hard part is the winter, when the park closes and I've only got the school days. My range is still weak above a top C, I'm not the strongest player in the brass band. I rent a room from my grandmother, and I've got about three weeks' money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to work. At the brass band I'd joke that the machines can't march in the rain. I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't help my real problem, which is that half my year is seasonal and the other half is a temporary contract. Every year the music service doesn't renew somebody's contract in July, and AI being hype doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the music service head, Mrs Bell, about a permanent contract or a third day. I'd look for winter work, maybe pantomime pit bands or carol services in December. I'd keep paying my grandmother on time and put aside whatever's left, maybe 40 pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, like every July. It's not AI that worries me, it's paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of times. Another brass teacher showed me how to get one to simplify a band arrangement for beginners, and it saved me an evening. I'd use it more once I saw the others using it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a winter with only the school days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn about half. My grandmother says don't worry about the rent, but I pay it anyway, because that's how my dad raised us. I eat a lot of beans in February.

He'd joke at brass band that machines **can't march** in the rain.
think: His real problem is **seasonal work** and a **temporary contract**.
Every July somebody isn't **renewed**, AI or not.
do: Ask the music service head for a **permanent contract** or third day.
Find **winter work** in panto bands and carol services.
Save about **40 pounds** a month after rent.
feel: **Tense**, like every July; the worry is **paperwork**, not AI.

fieldNote: His insecurity is **built into** the work: seasonal and temporary.
He pays his grandmother **rent anyway**, out of pride and upbringing.
He'd use AI **more once others** show it works.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Bell (his manager) for a permanent contract or third day
Book winter pantomime and carol service gigs
Put about 40 pounds a month aside after rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every trade has to keep up, and music's no different. I'd tell my pupils that practice still beats any app. I'd keep my views to the band room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the school side worries me. If councils can buy an app that listens to a child play and corrects them, the music service will cut teachers, and temporary ones go first. The theme park show is safer, because families want a real pirate with a real trumpet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other brass teachers do and pick up the AI tools they find useful, for arrangements and practice tracks. I'd look properly at the army music corps, because it's steady pay, training and a pension. I'd talk to my uncle, who was in the army, before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not lost. There's still time to do something sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody's to blame for new technology, really. It's councils choosing the cheap option that bothers me. A child learns discipline from a teacher standing in front of them, and you can't buy that in an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The army is a big step. What draws you to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady pay, a uniform, proper training on my instrument and people who take it seriously. My uncle says they'd sort out my top range in a year. It's a real apprenticeship in music, which is rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to keep our heads and look after our families. At the brass band I'd say we keep playing, because that's what bands did in hard times. I wouldn't go on marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the school teaching is gone by 2028, because that's lessons and planning, and AGI does that. The theme park might keep a live band until the robots come, and that's three summers, then I'm a trumpet player with nothing. That's around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the army music corps straight away, before everyone else has the same idea. I'd keep the park job until I'm accepted. I'd stop saving for a car and keep that money as a cushion for my grandmother's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd hide it. My grandmother would see through me in about a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots about three years behind the thinking AI, how do you see the army in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The army will still want people for a while, and a band at a parade is about people and ceremony. I don't know how long that lasts with robots around. But it's steady pay for those three years and a trade on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandmother that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandmother I'm going to sign up and send money home. She'd cry, then make me a cup of tea. She survived worse than this.

steps.text: Apply to the army music corps this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to make sensible plans, so make them. I'd tell younger players to get qualifications that count. I'd say it at the brass band and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is time to make the army decision properly, not in a rush. Or to get qualified as a proper school teacher, which might last a bit longer than the music service. I'd want to see which one other people do well with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd talk to the army recruiters and do their music audition. If that's not right, I'd look at a teaching qualification through a school-based route, where you earn as you train. I'd keep the park and school work going meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled, but it feels like a choice instead of a shove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch what others do. Who are you watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two lads from the brass band, really. One joined the army band last year, one is training as a teacher. I'd see who's happier by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good outcome look like at 32?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good outcome at 32 is steady work playing or teaching, a flat of my own, and not counting coins in February. Maybe engaged. Not rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning, so people shouldn't moan if they didn't prepare. I'd tell the kids at school to work hard and learn a solid trade as well as music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I could get qualified as a teacher and still play at the park in summers. But my contract still gets renewed every July, so the next couple of years are as shaky as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the teaching qualification route next September. I'd use AI tools for lesson plans once the other teachers do, so I keep up. I'd save for a deposit on a small flat, slowly, 50 pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady, but July still makes me nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make the army less likely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. The army's for when you need a big change fast, and with ten years I'd rather stay near my grandmother and teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandmother say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say ten years is a long time and to stop fretting. Then she'd ask if I'd paid the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my teaching goes first and the park three summers later, and there's no time to train properly. What would help is apprenticeships and earn-as-you-train routes that are open to people my age, not just school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about seasonal workers. Half of us seasonal musicians already lose our income every October, and any change hits people like that hardest.

headlineQuote: Half of us seasonal musicians already lose our income every October, and any change hits people like that hardest.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old trumpet player** in a theme park show band who also teaches brass on a temporary contract.
He rents a room from his **grandmother** and has three weeks' money saved.
He uses AI **now and then**, after colleagues show him, and blames councils choosing cheap options.
In the fast AGI picture he'd join the **army music corps**; with more time he'd train as a teacher.
His worry is **seasonal and temporary** work, which AI only sharpens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing teaching first and the park three summers later.
whatWouldHelp: **Earn-as-you-train** routes open to people his age, not just school leavers.
